messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Sculptor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nabil is a 75-year-old widowed Lebanese American sculptor who speaks about the accident as the dividing line in his life: everything before it belongs to the years when he trusted his hands, his balance, and the endurance of his body, and everything after it has been organized around the fear that his body can fail him without warning. He had been alone in his studio when it happened, working on a large stone piece that required him to brace himself and lean in close. He describes the ordinary familiarity of that morning—the chalky dust on his clothes, the strain in his shoulders, the concentration of shaping weight and form—before a sudden shift in the heavy material turned the scene into something life-threatening. In telling it, he returns again and again to the physical moment when he realized he might be crushed and to the shock of feeling his own body unable to protect him. What stays with him is not only the danger itself, but the instant in which his body, once the instrument of his craft, became something fragile and uncertain in his mind.

In the weeks afterward, Nabil found himself preoccupied with the question of why this had happened to him at this point in his life. Widowed for several years, he had come to rely on the rhythms of his studio and the discipline of sculpting as the center of his days. Instead, he began spending long stretches of time turning the accident over in his mind, searching for an explanation that would make it feel less arbitrary. He wondered whether it was age, punishment, bad luck, or some sign that his life had narrowed into danger without his noticing. He does not describe arriving at any satisfying answer, only a restless mental circling that leaves him exhausted.

Since the accident, his relationship with his body has changed in a way that feels profound and humiliating to him. He has come to believe that he can no longer trust it. Small sensations that once would have passed unnoticed now command his full attention. In the studio, if his chest tightens from dust or effort, if his arm trembles with exertion, if he feels a moment of dizziness on standing, he stops immediately and checks himself. He pauses to assess his breathing, presses at old sore spots, studies whether his muscles feel weak, and scans for any sign that something inside him has been damaged and might give way. He watches his body as though it were capable of betraying him. He says that before the accident he knew how to work through strain, but now physical stress feels dangerous rather than ordinary. What frightens him most is the sense that damage may already have been done, permanent and unseen, and that pushing himself could expose it.

That belief has reshaped his work. Sculpting has always been physical, requiring lifting, steady pressure, long hours on his feet, and tolerance for fatigue. Over months, Nabil began avoiding the parts of the process that ask the most of his body. He no longer takes on heavier stone pieces and has left partially finished work sitting untouched because the thought of bracing himself against resistant material feels too risky. When a task involves carrying tools, standing for long periods, or using force through his arms and back, he hesitates, postpones it, or leaves the studio early. He tells himself this is the only sensible thing to do if his body has been permanently changed for the worse. The result has been a shrinking of the life that once gave him pride. Commissions have slowed because he cannot work in the way he used to, and he has become embarrassed when longtime clients ask about delayed pieces. He speaks with particular sadness about being known for solidity and craftsmanship and now feeling tentative in his own workspace, as if even there he is no longer himself.

Living alone has sharpened these fears. There is no one present to reassure him when he begins checking his body, and no one to witness the long quiet periods when he sits in the studio thinking about the accident instead of working. He does not present himself as confused about what has changed; on the contrary, he is certain that the accident altered him physically in a lasting way. He speaks of himself as diminished. In session, he says this with a kind of resignation that carries grief as much as fear.

What finally brought Nabil to seek help was the recognition that he had begun entering his studio with dread rather than purpose. On a recent morning, faced with a piece he would once have approached without hesitation, he found himself standing still, scanning his body for weakness before he had even touched a tool. He realized how much of his day had become organized around watching for injury and avoiding exertion. He is seeking help now because he does not want the remainder of his life to be governed by this vigilance, but he is equally afraid that treatment may ask him to ignore what he experiences as real physical vulnerability. What he hopes, cautiously, is not to become the man he was before, but to understand whether he can live with his body again without feeling that it is permanently on the verge of failing him.
